sources.name: Federal Reserve Board, Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2019 to 2022: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (Federal Reserve Bulletin, Oct 2023), Table 4
sources.measures: Conditional median value of education installment loans (student debt) held by US families with any education loan debt, family (household) level, 2022 SCF wave
sources.notes: 21.8% of families held education loans in 2022. Text on p.26: 'Median balances decreased from $25,800 to $24,500, and mean balances decreased from $46,800 to $46,600.' The survey was fielded while most federal student loans were in pandemic zero-interest forbearance. The SCF sample is about 4,600 families, but the bulletin table does not state the n for the education-loan subsample.

sources.name: Federal Reserve Board, Survey of Consumer Finances 2019 wave, as restated in the Oct 2023 Federal Reserve Bulletin, Table 4
sources.measures: Conditional median value of education installment loans held by US families with any education loan debt, family level, 2019 SCF wave (inflation-adjusted to 2022 dollars)
sources.notes: This is the same survey and definition as the 2022 source, one wave earlier, so it is not independent. 21.5% of families held education loans in 2019.

definition: Conditional median value of education installment loans (student debt) held by US families with any education loan debt, family (household) level, 2022 SCF wave
caveat: The question asks about student loan debt in the US. The SCF measures it per family among families that hold education loans, not per individual borrower, and a family can contain more than one borrower. Among all families the median is $0, because only about 22% hold student debt. One comparison is the Federal Reserve SHED (Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024, May 2025, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-higher-education-and-student-loans.htm). It is individual-level and self-reported, counts debt for the respondent's own education only, and publishes the median only as a bracket: 'between $20,000 and $24,999'. It also reports that 28% of borrowers owed under $10,000 and most owed under $25,000. That puts it in line with the SCF, but it is a different unit of observation and is left out of sources. The Cleveland Fed Economic Commentary 2024-10 restates the SCF figures (about $25,000 median, $47,000 mean) and is not independent. The SCF is known to understate aggregate student debt relative to Fed G.19 and NY Fed credit-bureau totals, by roughly 25% in one secondary estimate. Neither official source publishes p90 or p99 values.

new_metric.label: Student loan debt
new_metric.definition: Outstanding balance of education loans (federal and private student loans) owed by a family that holds any such debt, as reported in the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances.
